notes.meaning: All people across the earth shared a single language and the exact same vocabulary. This shared speech preserved close human society after the great flood. While it made cooperation easy, humanity soon turned this gift toward united rebellion against God.

As people migrated across the region, they found a fertile river plain in the land of Shinar and made their home there. God had instructed Noah's descendants to spread out and fill the earth. Instead, the people chose to settle together in one place for their own convenience and security.

Because the flat plain had no building stone, the people molded clay bricks and baked them hard in kilns. They also used natural tar or asphalt as sticky mortar to hold the bricks together. Their readiness to tackle such hard work showed how determined they were to carry out their own selfish plans.

The people planned to construct a mighty city and a tower rising high toward the sky to make a lasting name for themselves. They hoped this monument would keep them together so they would never be scattered. Their goal showed proud self-reliance and open disobedience to God's command to populate the earth.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars often point out similarities between this text and ancient Babylonian building stories, seeing it as a direct challenge to Babylon's proud religious claims.

notes.meaning: The Lord came down to inspect the city and the tower that human hands were constructing. The Bible uses human terms here to show how small man's proudest projects appear from heaven. It also shows that God acts as a fair judge who examines the facts before executing judgment.

The Lord observed that a united people with one tongue would continue to devise worse evils without any restraint. Their shared language allowed sinful ideas to spread and multiply rapidly. God decided to intervene before their rebellious schemes caused even greater spiritual ruin.

God decided to confuse their speech so that they could no longer understand one another. The phrase 'let Us' points to the shared counsel of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This divine action peacefully ruined their proud project by removing their ability to cooperate.

The Lord scattered the builders from the plain across the face of the entire earth, bringing construction on the city to an end. What the people feared and tried to avoid came upon them as a direct consequence of their disobedience. God's judgment was also a mercy that forced mankind to fulfill His original plan to fill the world.

The site received the name Babel, which sounds like the Hebrew word for confusion, because God mingled their speech there. Those who sought world fame ended up remembered only for their failure and disgrace. This historic division of human tongues was later answered at Pentecost, where God's Spirit enabled people of every tongue to hear the gospel together.

This record traces the family line of Noah's son Shem starting two years after the flood, when he fathered Arphaxad at age one hundred. Shem lived another five hundred years and had other sons and daughters. God preserved this specific family line to prepare the way for His covenant promises and the future Messiah.

Arphaxad was thirty-five years old when he fathered Shelah, and he lived another four hundred and three years with more children. The gradual drop in human lifespans after the flood becomes visible in these verses. Through each generation, God's quiet care sustained the family that would carry His truth forward.

Shelah lived thirty years before fathering Eber, and he lived another four hundred and three years. Eber's name became linked with his descendants, who were later known as the Hebrews. God kept this lineage secure even as many other tribes drifted into spiritual darkness.

Eber became the father of Peleg at age thirty-four and lived another four hundred and thirty years. Peleg's name means division, marking the era when God divided mankind into different languages and lands at Babel. Eber outlived many of his descendants as an example of faithful endurance.

Peleg reached thirty years of age when he fathered Reu, and he lived another two hundred and nine years. During these generations, human life lengths dropped sharply to about half of what earlier ancestors had enjoyed. God steadily guided the chain of history toward the promises He planned to give.

Reu was thirty-two years old when he fathered Serug, and he lived for two hundred and seven more years. The biblical text records only names and ages here, moving quickly toward the story of Abram. God never lost sight of His chosen branch among the growing populations of the ancient world.

Serug lived thirty years before fathering Nahor, and he lived two hundred years after that. Each listed father represents another step toward the renewal of true worship on earth. Even in an era of widespread idolatry, God guarded the ancestral line of promise.

Nahor was twenty-nine years old when he became the father of Terah, and he lived another one hundred and nineteen years. Lifespans continued to grow shorter as modern history drew nearer. God's sovereign plan moved steadily toward the family that would receive His special calling.

Terah lived seventy years and became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Abram is mentioned first because of his special role in God's saving plan, even though he was likely born later than his brothers. This verse marks the bridge from world history to the personal story of the father of faith.

The family history now narrows directly onto Terah and his sons Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran became the father of Lot, who would later travel alongside Abram into Canaan. God was setting the stage for the specific people who would figure prominently in future covenant events.

Haran died before his father Terah while the family was still living in their homeland of Ur of the Chaldeans. Dying before one's parents was a painful sorrow that broke the normal course of life. Ur was an ancient city filled with the worship of false gods, showing the corrupt background out of which God called this family.

Abram and his brother Nahor chose wives from within their extended family circle. Abram married Sarai, while Nahor married his niece Milcah, the daughter of his deceased brother Haran. These domestic details explain the family connections that reappear later when Isaac and Jacob seek godly wives.

Sarai was barren and unable to bear any children. In that ancient culture, childlessness was a source of deep grief and social reproach. This personal tragedy set the stage for God to display His divine power by giving life where human hope had run out.

Terah took Abram, his grandson Lot, and Sarai, leaving Ur of the Chaldeans to travel toward Canaan. They stopped partway along the route at the town of Haran and settled there for an extended time. God had summoned Abram to leave his past behind, but the full journey paused during their stay in Haran.

Terah lived to be two hundred and five years old and died in Haran. His death marked the conclusion of that period of delay for Abram and his household. With his father gone, Abram was now ready to obey God's voice fully and step into the land of promise.
